core: working definition of the income statement, attributed to OpenStax's Principles of Accounting: a statement that shows the organization's financial performance for a given period of time, ending in profit or loss (corroborated by CFI: profit and loss over a period of time)
the shape: revenue at the top, expenses below, profit or loss at the bottom (net income or net loss), described in words
the simple arithmetic: revenue minus expenses equals net income or net loss (OpenStax formula), with an original bakery example
gross vs net: gross figures come before other items are subtracted (gross profit = revenue minus the direct cost of what was sold); net figures come after everything is subtracted (net income)
profit vs cash: the income statement shows earnings, not cash movements; the statement of cash flows is referenced as a sibling topic only
who reads it: owners, lenders, and investors, one line each on what each looks for
the honest framing: the income statement answers one question — did the business make money this period?
supporting: the statement is divided into time periods — monthly for internal reporting, aggregated into quarterly and annual results (CFI)
net income occurs when revenues and gains are greater than expenses and losses; net loss when the reverse (OpenStax 2.1)
the income statement is one of the core financial statements alongside the balance sheet and the statement of cash flows (CFI)

stakeholders as users of financial statements include investors, creditors, employees, managers, regulators, customers, and suppliers; a banker may study the statements to decide whether to lend (OpenStax 2.1)
outOfScope: revenue recognition detail and revenue types (owned by the revenue topic)
expense categories and cost detail (owned by the expenses topic)
the balance sheet's point-in-time picture of assets, liabilities, and equity (owned by the balance-sheet topic)
cash movements by operating, investing, and financing activities (owned by the statement-of-cash-flows topic)
ratio analysis and profitability metrics (owned by the financial-ratios topic)
statement preparation mechanics, journalizing, and the accounting cycle (owned by the accounting-cycle and journal-entries topics)
tax treatment of income and jurisdiction-specific rules

claims.claim: The income statement shows the organization's financial performance for a given period of time (OpenStax Principles of Accounting, Section 2.1); CFI describes it as one of a company's core financial statements that shows profit and loss over a period of time, summarizing all revenues and expenses to show the company's profit or loss for the period. The lesson's working definition follows OpenStax and is corroborated by CFI.

The income statement can be visualized by the formula Revenue − Expenses = Net Income/(Loss) (OpenStax Section 2.1); net income occurs when revenues and gains are greater than expenses and losses, and net loss occurs when expenses and losses are greater than revenues and gains.

The statement is shaped top to bottom: sales revenue is displayed at the very top of the income statement (CFI), expenses are listed below it (cost of goods sold, then operating and other expenses such as interest and taxes), and the final figure at the bottom is the net income or net loss (CFI: 'we finally arrive at the net income (or net loss)').

Gross profit is calculated by subtracting the cost of goods sold (or cost of sales) from sales revenue, before marketing, administrative, interest, and tax expenses are subtracted (CFI); net income is the figure after all other items on the statement have been deducted. The lesson states the distinction simply: gross comes before other items are subtracted, net comes after everything.

The income statement is divided into time periods that follow the company's operations, most commonly monthly for internal reporting, aggregated into quarterly and annual results (CFI); the period is therefore part of the statement's identity.

The income statement reports earnings, not cash movements: OpenStax's Section 2.1 example contrasts the statement's measure of performance with the checking-account balance and cash flows, and separately raises 'profit and positive cash flow' as distinct questions; CFI assigns the tracking of cash movements to the statement of cash flows. The lesson notes that profit and cash can move apart, and references the statement of cash flows as a sibling topic only.

Readers of the income statement include owners, lenders, and investors: OpenStax Section 2.1 lists investors and creditors among the stakeholders who use financial statements and gives the example of a banker interested in the financial statements to decide whether to lend to an organization; CFI describes the income statement as vital to investors and company management. The lesson gives one line per reader.

The honest framing — the income statement answers one question, did the business make money this period — follows from the net income/net loss definition (OpenStax) and the profit-or-loss-for-the-period definition (CFI); the lesson presents it as the reality check and routes broader questions (position, cash, ratios) to sibling topics.

conflictingEvidence.issue: Sources phrase the definition differently: OpenStax says the income statement shows the organization's financial performance for a given period of time; CFI says it shows profit and loss over a period of time, summarizing all revenues and expenses from operating and non-operating activities.
positions: OpenStax Principles of Accounting, Volume 1, Section 2.1: the income statement is 'a statement that shows the organization's financial performance for a given period of time.'

CFI Income Statement: the income statement 'shows their profit and loss over a period of time. It summarizes all revenues and expenses from both operating and non-operating activities to show the company's profit or loss for the period.'
conflictingEvidence.resolution: Both agree on the core: revenues and expenses over a period, ending in profit or loss. The lesson attributes the working definition to OpenStax's Principles of Accounting and notes CFI's corroboration; no single wording is reproduced verbatim.

conflictingEvidence.issue: The word 'gross' is used in more than one way: gross profit is revenue minus the cost of goods sold, while sales revenue itself is described by CFI as 'gross of the costs associated with creating the goods sold,' and 'net' can refer to net income or to net sales.
positions: CFI Income Statement: 'Gross Profit is calculated by subtracting Cost of Goods Sold (or Cost of Sales) from Sales Revenue.'
CFI Income Statement: sales revenue 'will be the gross of the costs associated with creating the goods sold or in providing services.'
conflictingEvidence.resolution: The lesson states the distinction simply — gross figures come before other items are subtracted, net figures after — and anchors it with the most common pair, gross profit and net income, avoiding the multiple narrower uses of the words.

conflictingEvidence.issue: Profit and cash are separate measures, and some readers treat net income as the change in the bank balance; OpenStax's own example shows the statement's measure differing from the checking-account story depending on when payments are made or received.
positions: OpenStax Section 2.1: the landscaping example contrasts earned revenue and expenses with the checking account balance, and the section treats 'profit and positive cash flow' as distinct questions.
CFI: the statement of cash flows is the statement that reports cash movements from operating, investing, and financing activities.
conflictingEvidence.resolution: The lesson states plainly that the income statement shows earnings, not cash movements, and references the statement of cash flows only as a sibling topic, per the subject's statement-shape guidance.
